summary: I have developed an interactive web app to detect exoplanets using public space telescope data and transit photometry. the tool addresses the challenge by letting users search target stars , download and clean light curves using python libraries like lightkurve, run Box Least Squares(BLS) period detection , and analyse phase-folded transit profiles through dynamic ploty charts and machine learning validation. This project is important because it transforms complex astrophysical data into an accessible , live-hosted dashboard. By bridging raw space data and interactive visualization ,it empowers citizens scientists and reseachers to explore the cosmos and uncover new planetary candidates effortlessly

What It Does & How It Works Project Exoseekers is an interactive web application that detects and validates exoplanet candidates using real space telescope observations from NASA's Kepler and TESS missions. Users can search for any target star to automatically retrieve stellar brightness data (light curves), remove instrumental noise and stellar variability, and run a Box Least Squares (BLS) periodogram to pinpoint periodic brightness dips caused by transiting planets. The application then phase-folds the light curve at the detected orbital period, renders interactive visualizations, and applies a Random Forest machine learning classifier to distinguish genuine planetary transits from false positives.

Tools, Languages & Resources Used

  • Programming & Prototyping: Python, Google Colab
  • Astrophysics & Data Processing: lightkurve, astropy, numpy (fetching public data from the NASA Exoplanet Archive and MAST)
  • Machine Learning: scikit-learn (Random Forest Classifier)
  • Frontend & Visualization: Streamlit, Plotly
  • Hosting & Version Control: GitHub, Streamlit Community Cloud
  • Benefits, Creativity & Intended Impact Analyzing raw astronomical light curves typically requires specialized software and command-line expertise. By wrapping NASA's open-source archives into an intuitive, browser-based dashboard, Project Exoseekers lowers the barrier to entry for students, educators, and citizen scientists. Instead of reading static data tables, users can interactively zoom into transit dips, test orbital periods, and experience firsthand how astrophysicists discover new worlds.

Key Factors Considered

  • Accessibility & Usability: Designed a clean interface that requires zero coding knowledge from the end user while keeping scientific visualizations interactive.
  • Signal-to-Noise Reliability: Combined classical astrophysical detrending and BLS periodograms with machine learning classification to reduce false-positive detections.
  • Google Gemini (a large language model) was used during development to assist with Python code generation, debugging, troubleshooting, and structuring project documentation.
